newsitem.title: USA: RJR's share of upfront tab "a shocker".
newsitem.headline: RJR's share of upfront tab "a shocker".

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp's estimate of $600 million as its share of the upfront payment in the tobacco litigation settlement agreement suprised analysts, who thought its portion would be much higher.

The five major U.S. tobacco companies agreed to an upfront payment of $10 billion as part of the sweeping agreement announced Friday. But since the announcement, investors have been waiting for the companies to disclose financial details specific to their own obligations.
RJR Nabisco has been "a very leveraged company," said Merrill Lynch analyst Allan Kaplan, who called the disclosure in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing "a shocker."
"People were concerned about how they would be able to borrow another $2.5 billion to pay this upfront payment. Now, suddenly, all they have to pay is $600 million."

Diana Temple, an anlyst at Salomon Brothers, said she upgraded her rating of RJR Nabisco shares last week after getting an indication their portion of the upfront payment would be lower than the $2.5 billion some thought was due.
"We did not expect it to be this low," Temple said.

During the settlement negotiations, the tobacco companies determined the upfront-payment obligations would be determined by market capitalization, according to an RJR spokesperson, with the balance of the payouts determined by market share.
RJR's spokesperson declined to comment further.

Asked how the companies decided to go with a payment structure that put so little pressure on RJR Nabisco, Temple said, "I think the industry did not want to put RJR in a situation where they would have to compete too viciously."

Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman elaborated, saying, "I think the upfront payment was really a private agreement between the tobacco companies. I think, in reality, it was based on what each company can afford."
Feldman said the slim portion of the upfront tab ascribed to RJR Nabisco was critical for the company to maintain investment-grade ratings on its current debt.
Philip Morris Cos Inc also filed a Form 8K with the SEC, but did not disclose what their portion of the payment would be.

Analysts estimates range from $6.7 billion to $7 billion. Philip Morris will finance the staggering amount through existing cash and cash-equivalent resources, through the reduction of share repurchases, and through an existing shelf registration for about $3 billion worth of debt.
"They (Philip Morris) will issue new debt, which the market will easily absorb," Feldman said.
Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, the parent of the No. 3 U.S. cigarette maker, Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp, will pay an estimated $1.7 billion, sources said.
The balance of the $10 billion will come from Loews Corp, the parent of Lorillard Tobacco Co, and smokeless tobacco king UST Inc.
